oldTown.title: Zemun Old Town Guide: Streets, Market & Café Culture
oldTown.description: A guide to Zemun's old town — the market, the lanes around Glavna, Gardoš and the café scene — and how it connects to the city park.
oldTown.cardDesc: The market, the lanes around Glavna, Gardoš and the café scene around the park.
oldTown.lead: Zemun's old town is the part of Belgrade that feels like a provincial Austrian town: cobbled lanes, a working market, and a tower with a view. It sits directly around the city park, and the two are best visited as one walk.

sections.title: Why it feels different
sections.body: Zemun was a separate border town until it became part of Belgrade, and it kept its own centre: low houses, courtyards and lanes laid out long before the capital's boulevards. The atmosphere is small-town rather than big-city, and the park is its green heart.

sections.title: Zemunska pijaca (the market)
sections.body: The market is the social centre of Zemun — produce, flowers, cheese and coffee under one roof, busiest in the morning. It is the natural place to pick up water, fruit or a quick breakfast, and it sits a few minutes' walk from the park.

sections.title: The lanes around Glavna
sections.body: Glavna and the side streets hold the old-town core: small galleries, craft shops, kafanas and terraces that fill in the evening. Wander without a plan — the grid is small, and every lane eventually reaches the market or the park.

sections.title: Gardoš and the view
sections.body: At the northern edge of the old town, Gardoš hill carries the tower — built around 1896 — whose balcony gives the classic panorama over the Danube and Belgrade beyond. The climb is short and steep; the reward is the widest view in Zemun.

sections.title: Linking up with the park
sections.body: The old town wraps around Zemun City Park on three sides. A good pattern: park first, then the lanes and market, then up to Gardoš, then down to the Danube — or the same loop in reverse if you arrive from the promenade.

faq.q: How far is the old town from the park?
faq.a: They touch — the old-town lanes begin a few minutes' walk from the park's edge.

faq.q: When is the market busiest?
faq.a: Morning, especially at weekends; it winds down in the early afternoon.

faq.q: What is Gardoš Tower?
faq.a: A lookout tower from around 1896 on Gardoš hill, with panoramic views over the Danube and Belgrade.

faq.q: Is the old town walkable?
faq.a: Yes — it is compact and flat apart from the short climb to Gardoš.

faq.q: Can I combine it with the park in one visit?
faq.a: That is the recommended way — see the half-day walking route.

promenade.title: From Zemun City Park to Zemunski Kej (Danube Promenade)
promenade.description: The short walk from Zemun City Park down to the Danube promenade (Zemunski kej) — the path, what you pass, and the best times for swans, riverboats and sunsets.
promenade.h1: From the Park to the Danube Promenade
promenade.cardDesc: The 10–15 minute walk down to Zemunski kej — the path, the stops, the sunsets.
promenade.lead: Zemunski kej — the Danube promenade — is a ten-to-fifteen-minute walk from the park, downhill through the old-town lanes. This page is about that specific path: where it starts, what you pass, and what to do when you reach the water.

sections.title: The path, step by step
sections.body: Leave the park on its eastern side and follow the lanes down towards the river — the route passes the edges of the old town and the market before opening onto the quay. It is an easy, mostly downhill walk of about 10–15 minutes; the return is the same in reverse, gently uphill.

sections.title: What you find on the quay
sections.body: A wide promenade runs along the Danube with benches, swans and the long view across to the Great War Island. Houseboats and riverboats are moored along the bank, and several floating restaurants serve grilled fish at the river's edge. It is Zemun's front terrace, busiest on warm evenings.

sections.title: Stopping points
sections.body: Benches face the water along the whole kej; the stretch near the moored boats is the liveliest, the stretch further along is quieter and better for sunsets. In warm weather the promenade fills after sunset — come early for the best seat.

sections.title: Sunset and seasons
sections.body: The promenade faces roughly west over the Danube, so sunsets colour the water and the far bank. Summer evenings are the peak; autumn and winter are quiet and clear, with river wind — bring a layer. The quay is exposed, so check the forecast before a long stroll.

sections.title: Practical notes
sections.body: The quay is a public promenade — free, open, no tickets. The path from the park is cobbled in places and includes a gentle slope; it is manageable for most walkers, though we cannot promise full wheelchair accessibility on every section. Combine this walk with the park and Gardoš using the half-day route.

faq.q: How far is the promenade from the park?
faq.a: About 10–15 minutes on foot, mostly downhill.

faq.q: What is there to eat on the kej?
faq.a: Several floating restaurants and cafés along the quay serve river fish and coffee — choose on the spot.

faq.q: Is the promenade good for sunsets?
faq.a: Yes — it faces the sunset over the Danube; arrive early for a bench.

faq.q: Are there swans?
faq.a: Yes — swans are a fixture of the Zemun riverbank.

faq.q: Is the walk suitable for strollers?
faq.a: Mostly — the lanes are cobbled and the slope is gentle, but check conditions if you use a wheelchair or stroller.
